name: Home laser hair removal

lead: Home laser hair removal devices use a low-energy diode laser to reduce hair growth, similar in principle to IPL but with a narrow wavelength. One cleared device was tested in a small trial that reported sustained reductions one year after treatment.
The same caveats as for IPL apply: the devices are suited mainly to dark hair on lighter skin, and results rest on small, often manufacturer-linked studies.

paras: Pigment in the hair absorbs the laser light and heats the follicle, damaging it to slow regrowth. Low energy per pulse means weekly or monthly sessions over months.

Burns, pigment change and eye injury are possible, especially on darker skin or with misuse. The most cited study (Wheeland 2012) had 13 participants and author ties to the manufacturer, and comparisons report that home devices achieve less than professional lasers. Long-term data are limited.

lead: Home laser hair removal refers to consumer devices that use a low-energy diode laser, applied by the user at home, to reduce unwanted hair growth. They work on the same general principle as professional laser systems and as home intense pulsed light (IPL) devices: pigment in the hair absorbs light, and the resulting heat is intended to damage the follicle so that regrowth slows [1][2]. Typical targets are the legs, underarms, bikini line, face and torso.

Professional laser hair removal has been described in dermatology reviews as an accepted method of long-term hair reduction, particularly for dark hair on lighter skin [1][3]. Reviews of hair removal practices note that most studies of efficacy have been limited to darker hair and fairer skin, and that all methods except electrolysis are classified as temporary [4]. A 2013 review concluded that the safety and efficacy of home-use devices needed further research [1].

Published evidence specific to home diode lasers is small. The best-known study, a 2012 trial of a home-use diode laser by Wheeland, followed 13 participants for a year after eight treatments and reported sustained hair reduction; the authors had ties to the manufacturer [5]. A 2026 analysis of manufacturer websites examined the safety information and adverse-event profiles that home laser devices present to consumers [6].

paras: Home laser devices are small handpieces that deliver pulses of near-infrared diode laser light through a window pressed against the skin. Compared with clinic systems they deliver lower energy per pulse, which is why manufacturers describe schedules of repeated sessions over several months rather than a short course [1].

Laser hair removal as a category is based on selective photothermolysis, in which light of a wavelength absorbed by melanin heats the pigmented hair and follicle while sparing most of the surrounding skin [2]. Professional systems include long-pulse alexandrite (755 nm), diode (around 810 nm), Nd:YAG (1,064 nm) and IPL devices [1]. Home devices are often distinguished from IPL by using a single narrow wavelength rather than broad-spectrum light; both types are sold for the same purpose.

Light absorbed by melanin in the hair shaft and follicle is converted to heat. Because hair grows in cycles and only follicles in the active growth phase are most susceptible, treatment is repeated at intervals so that more follicles are caught [2]. This is why reviews describe hair reduction developing over multiple sessions and why some regrowth can occur between and after courses [4][1].

The reliance on pigment is the main reason for the limits described in the literature: hair with little melanin (blond, grey, white or red) absorbs less light, and darker skin competes for the same light, increasing the risk of unwanted skin effects. A 2013 review stated that the longer-wavelength Nd:YAG laser is generally considered the better option for pigmented skin in a clinical setting [1], while a review of hair removal practices noted that efficacy data are mostly from dark hair on fair skin [4].

The evidence base for professional laser hair removal is considerably larger than that for home devices. Dermatology reviews report that in-office lasers provide a durable reduction in unwanted hair, and one older review described laser treatment as rivalling electrolysis for small areas and surpassing other modalities for large areas [1][3].

For home devices, the review literature is cautious. The 2013 review called for further research on safety and efficacy [1], and a 2019 paper in Lasers in Surgery and Medicine examined why light-based home-use devices work and how effective they are [7]. A 2023 PLOS ONE study compared a professional diode laser with a home-use IPL device for underarm hair reduction [8]. Hair-reduction figures quoted in marketing and in some encyclopedic summaries vary widely and depend on the device, the hair and skin type and the number of sessions.

Reviews of laser hair removal list temporary redness and discomfort as common, with rarer blistering, burns, pigment change, scarring and paradoxical increases in hair growth reported [1][2]. A 2026 analysis of commercial websites reviewed how this safety information is presented for home devices [6].

A case report published in 2022 described a full-thickness burn in a young woman associated with a do-it-yourself procedure during the COVID-19 lockdown in Ireland, illustrating the type of injury that can follow unsupervised use of energy-based devices [9]. A review of laser practice also noted that regulation and operator training vary between countries, which bears on professional rather than home use [2].

Guidance on patients taking isotretinoin has been the subject of a consensus review, which found limited evidence for the traditional advice to delay some procedures, though the recommendations are specific to clinical settings [10].

Selective photothermolysis was described by R. Rox Anderson and John A. Parrish in 1983 and underpins modern laser hair removal, according to a reference summary of the field [11]. Experimental work with ruby lasers on hair in the 1960s preceded the first US regulatory clearances for hair-reduction lasers in the mid-1990s, followed by alexandrite and diode systems in the late 1990s [11]. A 2002 review observed that laser hair removal had been controversial when first described but had become an accepted modality for long-term hair reduction [3].
Home-use light-based devices followed in the 2000s and 2010s. The 2012 home diode-laser trial by Wheeland, cited above, is one of the earliest peer-reviewed studies of such a device [5].

Within appearance-focused communities, hair removal is discussed as part of grooming of the body, face and neck, and home lasers are generally positioned as a lower-cost alternative to clinic courses. Commonly raised themes include suitability for particular hair and skin colours, the number of sessions needed and comparisons with IPL and electrolysis. The wiki's own rating describes diode home lasers as having similar caveats to IPL devices.

A 2012 study in Lasers in Surgery and Medicine tested a home-use diode laser in a small group of 13 participants, reporting sustained hair reduction one year after eight treatments; the authors had ties to the manufacturer [5]. A 2023 trial compared a professional diode laser with a home-use IPL device on the underarm [8], and a 2019 review discussed the efficacy of light-based home devices [7].

Studies of professional diode lasers include a 2001 clinical trial in patients with dark skin [12], a randomized trial of pain control with ice packs or topical anesthetic during 810 nm diode underarm treatment [13], and a randomized trial comparing shaving with clipping before laser sessions in women with hirsutism [14]. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis examined laser hair removal for hidradenitis suppurativa across ten studies with 227 patients [15]. These studies concern professional devices or other conditions rather than consumer devices.
